event: VXE 930 (Adv Nav, MOLSON) repeatedly showed a 'one or more VTOL sensors failed' fault at the Shield Pitot step of the launch wizard; on one launch after the fault cleared the aircraft gave low battery warnings and was recovered safely.
component: NovAtel INS heading estimate versus FWAP and VTOL AP heading (launch wizard sensor agreement check)
failure_mode: NovAtel INS heading drifted away from the FWAP and VTOL AP heading on the ground, the launch wizard flagged the disagreement as a VTOL sensor failure
contributing: motion and wind during initialization
heading updates to the NovAtel too slow, no filter reset on large disagreement
mixed firmware versions on the aircraft (XCOMM 6.5.1, VTOL and SUAV 6.5.0)
battery warning on the same flight split to VXEP-1557

evidence.quote: the ‘vtol sensor failures’ are caused by a disagreement between the novatel heading and the fwap/vtol ap.
NovAtel heading drift is causing some ‘VTOL SENSOR FAULT’ failures during launch wizard.
If novatel heading disagrees with fixed-wing heading by more than 10 degrees, reset the filter state.
Resolved in apex builds with faster and lower uncertainty heading updates.
the launch wizard will prevent launch if the disagreement is greater than 20 degrees

team_root_cause: Motion during initialization can cause the INS to disagree with the fixed-wing and vtol processors.  This results in a VTOL sensor fault that is difficult to understand/repair.

would_settle_it.what: NovAtel heading versus FWAP and VTOL AP heading during the launch wizard, to confirm the size of the disagreement and whether the aircraft was moved during initialization

reasoning: Eric Brewer reviewed the AAR and states the VTOL sensor failures came from a disagreement between the NovAtel heading and the FWAP/VTOL AP. The linked test ticket FS2-3760 confirms NovAtel heading drift causes these launch wizard faults and the fix was faster heading updates and a filter reset when the headings disagree. The mechanism is named from log review, but why the heading drifted (motion at initialization versus slow updates) is not separately proven, so confidence is medium.
notes: The battery warning after takeoff on the same flight was split into VXEP-1557; David Grosher notes the battery checker used an incorrect chemistry model. Similar faults later reported on VXE 928 and VXE 933 (VXEP-1774, not read). The team Root Cause field contains a double space, copied as written.

event: VXE 863 (USBP) cut its VTOL lift motors a few seconds into the landing descent after a 2.5 hour flight, pitched into a dive and glide landed into a bush about 2,000 ft from the landing zone, damaging the elevator and tail.
component: XCOMM firmware (watchdog reset, dynamic memory allocation in file I/O)
failure_mode: XCOMM watchdog reset in flight upset the landing logic (baro offset jump near the reset), the system went from descent to LAND_COMPLETE almost immediately and safed the lift motors in the air
contributing: this XCOMM had a second watchdog reset during an earlier investigation, suggesting board-level susceptibility
VXEP-1692 links XCOMM watchdog resets to on-board 12V and 6V power converters and memory corruption
no GCS warning or popup at the event

evidence.quote: It looks like there was a WDT on the XCOMM which led to a 2nd datalog in the XCOMM that wasn’t included in the AAR package.
The system transitioned into descent and then LAND_COMPLETE almost immediately. This is very strange.
It seems like the landing was detected prematurely resulting in the lift motors being safed.
The root cause was an xcomm watchdog reset, Dave advises we have seen 5-10 watchdog resets with the latest software but haven’t traced root cause.
Turning off all 12V and 6V converters on a XCOM with a lot of WDs (Rate ~6/hr before) eliminated them over a 3 day period.
Some exceptions seen. Trigger for those is most likely memory corruption.

team_root_cause: Watchdog reset on xcomm processor caused invalid detection of landing state.

would_settle_it.what: XCL00098.csv and event logs around CPU time 2138 to confirm the WD BOOT timing against the LAND_COMPLETE transition and baro offset jump
Eric Brewer's slides tying the watchdog reset to the premature landing detection
burn-in or power converter check of the removed XCOMM to see whether it is one of the watchdog-prone boards

attachments_read: 41388_PS ASSET 260127 Edge USBP Bailment Warranty Repair VXE863 ASSET-04.xlsx.md
reasoning: David Grosher's log review shows an XCOMM watchdog reset in flight, followed by an almost immediate change from descent to LAND_COMPLETE, so the landing was detected prematurely and the lift motors were safed. The baro offset jump near the reset time is the likely path from the reset to the false landing detection. Why the XCOMM reset is still open: the ticket's corrective action targets firmware memory allocation, while VXEP-1692 also implicates the XCOMM power converters, so the mechanism is determined but the reset's own cause is medium confidence.
notes: RMA-820 holds only repair quotes and an image-only intake PDF (no text), no teardown findings; repairs were airframe parts (center wing, wing tips, servo, saddle bondment). FS2-3882 was canceled because the investigation was done elsewhere. VXEP-1978 (later loss of link on 863) was not read.

event: VXE 593 (MOLSON, fuel cell configuration) aborted its launch when the VTOL magnetometer was declared failed during the climb and landed safely; afterwards the fuel cell was found smoking inside the nose.
component: VTOL AP magnetometer (magnetic disturbance during lift spool-up)
failure_mode: large magnetometer disturbance began as the lift system spooled up, corrupted the VTOL attitude estimate and led to the abort; magnetometer then correctly declared failed
contributing: takeoff from a concrete pad with probable rebar
possible electrical interference from the VTOL system, fuel cell or E140 ground loop
fuel cell smoking after landing (cloned to VXEP-1586)

evidence.quote: there is a pretty significant disturbance in the mag readings right when the vtol system spools up.
I would have thought potentially an environmental issue (i.e. mag disturbance on the runway) but this doesn’t really track since the disturbance follows the vehicle up 100'.
the mag did not have the large disturbance that we observed during the abort.
That likely points to the issue with the fuel cell being related to the mag disturbance.
They moved 100 feet from original location (concrete pad) into grass for this most recent flight.

team_root_cause: Looking at AAR from flight on 17Oct2025, there seems to be no anomalies or mag/IMU issues. We have decided to BT this as there was most likely rebar or some type of metal in the concrete pad that was flown from when the abort occurred.
disagreement: The team closed this as rebar in the concrete pad, and the later clean flight from grass supports that. But Eric Brewer found the disturbance "follows the vehicle up 100'" and started only after the throttles ramped, and he also wrote "That likely points to the issue with the fuel cell being related to the mag disturbance." The evidence narrows the abort to an external magnetic disturbance on the VTOL magnetometer without settling between the pad and an on-board electrical source.

would_settle_it.what: mag magnitude versus lift throttle and altitude during the abort, to see whether the disturbance falls off with height (pad) or tracks current (on-board source)
mag readings versus lift and fuel cell currents during the abort
fuel cell D4500799 findings from RMA-973 that could tie the fuel cell fault to the mag disturbance

reasoning: The abort worked as designed after the VTOL magnetometer input degraded, so it is scored on the magnetometer. The disturbance started at lift spool-up and followed the aircraft to 100 ft, which argues against a pure ground source, while a later flight from grass was clean, which supports the pad. With two credible sources and no test separating them, the cause is narrowed only.
notes: Ticket was closed as Cannot Reproduce and put on the Bermuda Triangle list. The fuel cell smoking part was cloned to VXEP-1586, which ended with the fuel cell RMAd for a separate HLB charging failure (RMA-973 not in export).

event: VXE B35X 881 (LRR internal asset) lost power to the forward motor and servos on the ground when the Orbital drop kit PMM was connected; function returned when the PMM was unpowered or the aircraft power cycled.
component: Orbital drop kit PMM on Aux payload port 2
failure_mode: connecting or running the Orbital PMM caused loss of power to the forward (cruise) motor and the servos
contributing: heavy configuration (47.6 lb) with HPMB, two PRMs and two DGMs
intermittent: reappeared about 10 minutes after reconnecting

evidence.quote: With aircraft powered on the aircraft lost power to the forward motor and the servos upon connecting the PMM.
PMM was disconnected via securing Aux payload port 2 power.
After about 10 minutes, Launch Wizard was started and the aircraft had lost power to the front prop again, noticed upon front prop test in Launch Wizard.
Orbital equipment was disconnected and launch wizard was conducted to the point of Arm/ Launch with no abnormalities.

would_settle_it.what: XCOMM event logs and power rail or payload port current at the moments the forward motor and servos dropped out
VTOL side logs for the same events

would_settle_it.file: Orbital PMM and Aux payload port 2
would_settle_it.what: bench test of the PMM load on Aux port 2 for overcurrent or a short that trips the shared power to the cruise motor ESC and servos

reasoning: The loss of forward motor and servo power appeared when the PMM was connected, cleared when Aux payload port 2 power was secured, and did not occur with the Orbital equipment removed. That points to the PMM or its power path on Aux port 2, but no log or bench result names the part or mechanism, so it is narrowed to the payload.
notes: No investigation results were recorded; the only comment says the aircraft has flown since. Tail taken from 'VXE B35X SN 881' in the description.

contributing: heavy configuration with E140 gimbal

event: VXE 828 (LRR Block 35X) dropped 30 to 40 ft during the fixed wing to VTOL transition before the lift props fully took over, then landed normally.
component: lift motor start delay after low throttle on transition (VTOL AP command processing with ESC firmware settings, as in VXEP-426)
failure_mode: lift motors held at low throttle because the aircraft was above target altitude, then a wind disturbance demanded thrust and one motor responded about 0.75 s late
contributing: high winds
aircraft above target altitude at transition so lift throttles were low
low GPS CNO and satellite count near transition (not shown to matter)

evidence.quote: It looks like the lift motors are on but low throttle because we are actually above the target altitude.
CAN looks fine. This looks like a case of the motor delay after the LR throttle was low on transition.
It may be related to that issue as there was a delay for about 0.75 seconds on one of the motors.
Having said that the altitude loss appears to be expected.
VTOL AP process of commands to motors with existing configuration and settings in ESC FW is causing a delay.  See report for details.

disagreement: The team closed this as "Aircraft behaved as expected." But Eric Brewer wrote "This looks like a case of the motor delay after the LR throttle was low on transition" and David Grosher linked it to VXEP-426, noting "a delay for about 0.75 seconds on one of the motors". VXEP-426 treats that delay as a real VTOL AP and ESC firmware issue, so the drop is better read as wind plus a known motor start delay than as fully normal behavior.

would_settle_it.what: lift throttle versus motor current on transition, showing which motor lagged and by how much
per motor throttle, current and VTOL motor state flags during the transition

reasoning: David Grosher found the lift motors at low throttle because the aircraft was above its target altitude, then a wind disturbance made them ramp up. Eric Brewer then identified a motor delay after the LR throttle had been low, and Grosher measured about 0.75 s on one motor and tied it to the VXEP-426 slow start issue. The drop is narrowed to wind plus the known lift motor start delay, with low confidence because the team judged the altitude loss expected.
notes: 'LR' mapped to motor 4 (rear left) by the convention; Eric's wording ties the delay to the LR throttle but Grosher only says 'one of the motors', so the position is not fully certain. VXEP-426 converted pptx attachments were not read (relates link only). Aircraft 828 is also in VXEP-1569 and VXEP-1880 for LEMB CAN dropouts; Eric found CAN fine on this flight.

event: VXE 818 (LRR Block 35X with LEMB) kept its VTOL lift motors running after the transition to fixed wing, descended behind a tree line and crashed.
component: LEMB battery controller (BMS) board CAN TVS diodes (D14 CANH, D10 CANL)
failure_mode: damaged TVS diodes on the LEMB BMS CAN node pulled the CAN differential voltage down, causing about 6 s of dropped CAN messages; the VTOL missed the XCOMM ASSIST transition message so the lift system never braked and safed
contributing: 35X configuration ground loop through the LEMB data cable creates transients above the diode ratings
CAN bus over-terminated (XCOMM, VTOL AP and ADB)
XCOMM to VTOL SAFE messages not acknowledged (FS2-2320 never implemented)
backup safe logic did not trigger
VTOL put in RC mode just before launch completion

evidence.quote: It appears that the VTOL was not getting some updates over CAN for about 6 seconds during the final portion of the transition.
It specifically missed a message to transition to ASSIST which starts the counter for brake and safe of the lift system.
Traced to bad CAN bus performance with specific LEMBs.
When B35x battery CAN node is connected to the rest of the architecture, it pulls down the CAN differential voltage to between 1V to 1.4V.
It has been determined that the TVS diodes on the battery controller are either malfunctioning, installed backwards, or damaged.
we were able to demonstrate that the 35X configuration causes transients that exceed the component ratings on the diodes that failed.

team_root_cause:
Damage to LEMB circuits due to transients created noise on the CAN bus, which led to dropped communicaiton. 
- Vehicle investigation https://jenaero.sharepoint.com/:p:/r/sites/FlightSafety/_layouts/15/Doc.aspx?sourcedoc=%7BCC45616B-191B-4D74-A492-B4394C3879F9%7D&file=V818IncidentInvestigation.pptx&action=edit&mobileredirect=true
- LEMB investigation: https://jenaero.sharepoint.com/:p:/r/sites/FlightSafety/_layouts/15/Doc.aspx?sourcedoc=%7BCC45616B-191B-4D74-A492-B4394C3879F9%7D&file=V818IncidentInvestigation.pptx&action=edit&mobileredirect=true

would_settle_it.what: V818IncidentInvestigation.pptx, to confirm which LEMB serial was on 818 for the crash flight
CAN error rate with the LEMB on the bus

reasoning: The flight logs show the VTOL lost CAN updates for about 6 s and missed the ASSIST message that starts lift system brake and safe, so the motors kept running. The team traced the CAN dropouts to the LEMBs, and VXEP-1880 bench tests found returned LEMB BMS boards pulling the CAN differential down with damaged TVS diodes and transients above their ratings in the 35X configuration. The failure was not recreated and the specific LEMB on 818 is not named, so confidence is medium.
notes: The converted LRR 25 ID Mishap PDF is a blank reporting form with no incident details. XKIT-5172 covers B40 ESC CAN errors (SJW timing), a separate issue on a different block. The two SharePoint links in the Root Cause field point to the same file. Misspelling 'communicaiton' copied as written.
